newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries rally, budget pact hopes spur gains.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries rally, budget pact hopes spur gains.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were higher at midday on Wednesday, bouyed by budget hopes.
Optimism that a U.S. budget agreement could be reached stirred again in the market in late morning trade, enabling prices to erase early losses and rally further, analysts said.

Prices opened lower and augmented mild early losses after the government reported that Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew 5.6 percent in the first quarter, a higher number than the market had expected. But buyers entered on the dip and losses gradually were trimmed.
"It seems that the latest gains are probably due to the budget talk," said Elliott Platt, managing director and head of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
"People who were not focused on the budget battle suddently hear this buzzword of a balanced budget deal and they're getting excited about it," said Platt.
U.S. Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said before midday on Wednesday that he believed budget negotiators were "very close" on reaching an agreement with the White House.
In early afternoon trade, the benchmark 30-year bond was up 17/32 to 96-1/32, its yield at 6.94 percent.

"I think it's (the budget talks) and also that there were just a lot of people waiting to buy a dip this morning, having missed out yesterday when the move up (after the Employment Cost Index and durable goods reports) was so sudden," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co.
"Once the buying started, there just wasn't a whole lot to stand in its way," said Youngdahl.
Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A., said the market could encounter some overhead resistance at 6.93 percent on the long bond yield.
Platt said a lot of previously existing shorts are being reversed and that players who were waiting for a 7-1/4-percent long bond yield before buying "now have to get in."

"The fear of this week's data has been replaced by the fear of being underinvested," said Aubrey G. Lanston's Youngdahl. "The psychology change occurred yesterday with the ECI and it's continuing today. People have money to put to work, and that's what they're doing."
Platt said participants have started to believe that the economy's growth will now start to slow.
Platt forecast GDP growth of 2.6 percent for the second quarter, 2.0 percent for the third quarter and 2.0 percent for the fourth quarter.

"People who had been on the edge of their seats expecting disaster are now starting to see stuff that looks pretty enticing," he said. Platt called a four percent real rate of return on the long bond "historically high" and said a strong dollar, weak European economies and an "overvalued" stock market were also positive factors for bonds.
Besides the GDP data, the market also saw a dip in the Chicago PMI and in that index's prices paid inflation item.
Three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.10 percent and six-month bill rates were up two basis points to 5.31 percent. Year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.57 percent.
Two-year notes were up 3/32 to 100-6/32, yielding 6.27 percent. Five-year notes were up 9/32 to 100-8/32, yielding 6.57 percent. Ten-year notes were up 13/32 to 96-25/32, yielding 6.70 percent.
